items.title: Cutting an integral into 100 trapezoids beats analytical integration for most real problems
items.claim: Most integrals appearing in physics, engineering or statistics do NOT have closed-form solutions. They're computed numerically. The simplest method (trapezoidal rule) divides the interval into strips and approximates each as a trapezoid.

options.text: Error in the trapezoidal rule is O(1/n^2) where n is the number of strips. Simpson's rule (quadratic interpolation) is O(1/n^4). Gauss-Legendre and adaptive quadrature can achieve essentially machine precision for well-behaved integrands
Always less accurate than analytical answers

items.reveal:
Trapezoidal rule: approximate integral from a to b of f(x) dx by the sum of trapezoidal strips. Error scales as h^2 (where h is the strip width), so halving h quarters the error.

Simpson's rule (uses quadratic fits to triples of points): error scales as h^4. Halving h reduces error by 16x.

For a function smooth enough on [a, b], Simpson's rule with 20 strips can give 6-7 decimal places of accuracy. Gauss-Legendre quadrature with 10 nodes can give 10-15 decimal places.

Many real-world integrals:
- integral of e^(-x^2) dx: no elementary antiderivative. Used everywhere in statistics. Always computed numerically (or via the error function erf).
- integral of sin(x)/x dx: no elementary form. Defined as the sine integral Si(x).
- integral over irregular domains, multidimensional integrals, integrals with singularities — numerical methods are standard.

Monte Carlo integration: for high-dimensional integrals (d > ~4), grid-based methods (Simpson, Gauss) suffer the 'curse of dimensionality' — n grid points per axis means n^d total. Monte Carlo (random sampling) has error O(1/sqrt(N)) independent of dimension; the standard tool for integrals in 10+ dimensions (e.g., statistical mechanics, finance).

More sophisticated: adaptive quadrature (refines where the function is wiggly), Romberg's method, Chebyshev quadrature for analytic functions, sparse grids, quasi-Monte Carlo with low-discrepancy sequences (Sobol, Halton).

The trade-off between numerical and analytical: analytical is exact when available, but unavailable for most functions. Numerical is universally applicable, with accuracy dialed up by computational cost.
items.why: Calculus class focuses on analytical integration. Real applied math is largely numerical — and the numerical methods can be vastly faster and more accurate than the analytical ones for the integrals actually needed.

items.title: Achilles can never catch the tortoise
items.claim: Zeno's paradox: Achilles gives the tortoise a head start. To catch it, he must reach where the tortoise was — by then the tortoise has moved a bit. Repeat infinitely. He performs infinitely many tasks and can never reach the tortoise.

options.text: Achilles is actually slower than the tortoise
Infinitely many finite tasks can take finite total time — the geometric series 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 + ... sums to 1, not infinity

items.reveal_title: Zeno's paradoxes and the calculus that resolves them
items.reveal:
Zeno of Elea (c. 490-430 BC) offered several paradoxes about motion:
- Dichotomy: to walk across a room, you must first walk half-way, then half of what remains, etc. Infinite steps.
- Achilles and the tortoise: as above.
- Arrow: at each instant, an arrow occupies a fixed position, so it isn't moving — yet motion sums to a journey.

Resolution requires the concept of convergent infinite series — formalised in the 17th and 19th centuries by Newton, Leibniz, Cauchy and Weierstrass. The sum 1 + 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 + ... equals 2, not infinity. Infinitely many tasks can be completed in finite time, provided their durations form a convergent series.

The paradoxes pre-dated rigorous calculus by 2000 years. Zeno's challenge actually pushed mathematicians toward developing the tools needed to handle infinity and the continuum properly. Mathematicians sometimes joke that Zeno was the first calculus student to fail to grasp limits.
items.why: Common sense rules out infinite tasks in finite time. Mathematical analysis shows infinite tasks of decreasing size can totalise to finite quantities — and motion proceeds.

items.title: Centrifugal force doesn't exist — except when it does
items.claim: Physics teachers often say 'centrifugal force isn't real'. In an inertial reference frame, that's correct — only centripetal force exists. But in a ROTATING frame (sitting in a car going round a corner), centrifugal force is a genuine, calculable, predictive force.
items.prompt: What's the relationship between the two?

options.text: They are the same force renamed

Centripetal force is the inward force that keeps an object circling (real in any frame); centrifugal force is the apparent OUTWARD force in a rotating frame — fictitious in inertial frames but necessary for Newton's laws to hold in rotating ones
Only one of them is real, but textbooks disagree which

items.reveal:
Newton's laws hold in inertial (non-accelerating) frames. To make them hold in a rotating (accelerating) frame, you must add fictitious forces — apparent forces that arise from the frame's acceleration, not from any physical interaction.

In a rotating frame at angular velocity omega, two fictitious forces:
- Centrifugal: F = m * omega^2 * r, outward.
- Coriolis: F = -2 m omega cross v, perpendicular to motion.

For a passenger in a car going around a curve at constant speed:
- Inertial (road) frame: the only real force is the inward (centripetal) friction from the seat. The car turns; the passenger tends to continue straight, hence pushes against the door.
- Rotating (car) frame: the passenger feels pushed outward — centrifugal force. The frame is accelerating; the passenger needs to invoke centrifugal force to make Newton's laws work.

Both descriptions give the same observable outcome. The 'centrifugal' force is real in the car's frame in the sense that you must include it to do correct mechanics; it's 'fictitious' in the road's frame in the sense that no physical object is pushing.

Earth's rotation: Coriolis force (small at human scales) deflects winds and ocean currents — counterclockwise around northern lows, clockwise around southern lows. The Earth's frame is rotating; the Coriolis force must be included.

In general relativity, all forces of inertia (centrifugal, Coriolis, gravity) become 'fictitious' in the right sense — geometry of spacetime, not push-pull.
items.why: The 'centrifugal is fictitious' rule is true in one frame but missing the point. Both forces are correct in their proper frames. The debate is about reference-frame choice, not physics.
